message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of tasks:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from operating system tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel processing – originally built to render graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) optimized for low latency, complex branching, and high single‑thread performance. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput and executing many identical operations simultaneously. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) with sophisticated control flow, caching, branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution. | Simpler, often SIMD‑style instructions that can run the same operation on many data elements at once. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2 caches per core, deep memory hierarchy, sophisticated prefetching. | Smaller per‑core cache; relies on massive bandwidth from shared memory (VRAM). |
| **Typical Workloads** | Tasks that require quick responses to varied instructions (e.g., web browsing, office apps, OS services). | Data‑parallel workloads: rendering frames, matrix multiplications, convolutional neural nets, simulations. |
| **Performance Metrics** | Measured in FLOPS per core, clock speed, IPC (instructions per cycle). | Measured in total FLOPS, memory bandwidth, number of shader/compute units. |
| **Energy Efficiency** | Optimized for power‑constrained mobile CPUs, but still higher power per core than GPUs. | Very efficient at high throughput per watt for parallel tasks. |
| **Programming Model** | Single‑threaded or multi‑threaded code written in C/C++, Java, etc.; uses OS scheduling. | Parallel programming models like CUDA, OpenCL, DirectX compute shaders; requires explicit thread/block organization. |

In short, a CPU excels at handling diverse, sequential tasks quickly, while a GPU shines when you need to perform the same operation on a huge amount of data simultaneously. That’s why modern systems combine both: the CPU manages overall control flow, and the GPU accelerates heavy‑lifting computations.
